column1: How do you celebrate Independence Day? How do you celebrate Independence Day? For me, it’s a time of reflection, a moment to consider the paradoxes of freedom and the cost of liberty. I often find myself revisiting the words of the Founding Fathers, not as infallible prophets, but as flawed men who dared to dream of a nation built on principles they themselves struggled to fully embody. I read the Declaration of Independence, not as a sacred text, but as a human document, riddled with contradictions—its bold assertion of equality juxtaposed against the silence on slavery. I think of Frederick Douglass’s searing question: “What, to the American slave, is your Fourth of July?” And I wonder how far we’ve truly come.    I don’t celebrate with fireworks or parades. Instead, I light a candle, a quiet nod to the enduring flame of hope that flickers even in the darkest times. I read poetry—Whitman’s “I Hear America Singing,” Hughes’s “Let America Be America Again,” and Dunbar’s “We Wear the Mask.” These voices remind me that America is not a monolith but a chorus, sometimes harmonious, often dissonant, but always striving toward something greater.    I also take time to honor those who’ve fought for freedom in ways that history often overlooks—the suffragettes, the civil rights activists, the labor organizers, the LGBTQ+ pioneers. Their struggles remind me that independence is not a gift but a battle, one that requires vigilance and courage.    And yes, I grill. Because even in the midst of reflection, there’s room for joy, for community, for the simple pleasure of sharing a meal with loved ones. But as I bite into that burger, I remember the words of Thomas Paine: “Those who expect to reap the blessings of freedom must, like men, undergo the fatigue of supporting it.” So, I celebrate with gratitude, but also with a resolve to keep fighting for a more just and equitable America. Because independence, like faith, is not a destination but a journey. —Michael R. Burch

God is real. Atheists how can you prove me wrong? God is real. Atheists, how can you prove me wrong? When faced with such a question, I often find myself reflecting on the nature of belief itself. Belief in God, for many, is an act of faith—an intuitive, deeply personal conviction that transcends empirical evidence. But what of those who demand proof? Can the existence of God, or the lack thereof, be validated through logic, reason, or scientific inquiry alone? I’m reminded of my own journey, steeped in the evangelical Christian traditions of my youth, where the Bible was presented as the ultimate authority. Yet, as I delved into its pages, I encountered contradictions, moral quandaries, and narratives that seemed more human than divine. The Genesis account of creation, for instance, clashes with the findings of modern cosmology. The God who orders genocide in the Old Testament appears at odds with the loving deity preached in the New. These discrepancies, among others, led me to question not only the veracity of the Bible but the very existence of the God it portrays.   But let us entertain the question further: how *can* atheists prove God’s nonexistence? The burden of proof, some would argue, lies not with the skeptic but with the believer. If God is real, where is the tangible evidence? Where are the miracles, the undeniable signs of divine intervention, the irrefutable answers to prayer? For that matter, why does evil persist in a world governed by an all-powerful, all-loving deity? The problem of suffering, as articulated by philosophers like Epicurus, remains a formidable challenge to theistic belief. If God is both willing and able to prevent evil, why does evil exist? If He is neither willing nor able, is He truly God? These are not idle questions but profound, existential inquiries that demand thoughtful responses.  And yet, belief persists. For some, it is a source of comfort, meaning, and moral guidance. For others, it is an inherited tradition, a cultural cornerstone, or a shield against the unknown. But belief, in and of itself, does not constitute proof. To demand that atheists disprove the existence of God is to shift the burden of proof unfairly. After all, one cannot disprove the existence of something for which there is no evidence. The onus is on the believer to provide compelling reasons for their faith, not on the skeptic to debunk an unsubstantiated claim.  So, to the question at hand: God is real. Atheists, how can you prove me wrong? The answer is simple: we cannot, nor must we. It is not our task to disprove what has not been proven in the first place. Instead, we ask only for the same intellectual rigor and skepticism applied to other areas of life. If God exists, let the evidence speak. If not, let us continue to seek truth, not in the shadow of dogma, but in the light of reason and inquiry.

What stories in the Bible had the biggest impact on you? The stories in the Bible that had the biggest impact on me are the ones that reveal the darker, more troubling aspects of its morality. Take the tale of Noah’s Ark, for instance. On the surface, it’s a story of divine salvation and renewal. But dig deeper, and you’ll find a narrative drenched in indiscriminate destruction. Jehovah drowns millions of human beings—men, women, children, infants, and even unborn babies—alongside countless innocent animals. The sheer scale of this carnage is staggering, yet it’s often glossed over in favor of the comforting image of a rainbow covenant. What kind of god resorts to such brutality? And why is this being, who claims to be all-loving and all-merciful, so quick to unleash such utter devastation?  Then there’s the story of Abraham and Isaac. Here, Jehovah tests Abraham’s faith by commanding him to sacrifice his own son. The narrative is often praised for its demonstration of Abraham’s unwavering devotion, but it’s equally a story of moral bankruptcy. What kind of deity demands such a horrific act? And what does it say about a faith that celebrates blind obedience over compassion and reason? The fact that Abraham was willing to kill his son, only to be stopped at the last moment by an angel, raises disturbing questions about the nature of divine commands and human morality.  The Book of Job is another example. Job, a righteous man, is subjected to unspeakable suffering to satisfy a wager between Jehovah and Satan. His children are killed, his health is destroyed, and his possessions are stripped away—all to prove a point. The story ends with Job being “restored” with new children, as if they were mere replaceable objects. The theological implications are chilling: human suffering is reduced to a cosmic game, with Jehovah as the indifferent puppet master.  These stories, among others, forced me to confront the darker truths embedded in the Bible. They made me question the morality of a god who claims to be just and loving, yet acts with such capricious cruelty. If faith is supposed to uplift and inspire, why do these narratives leave so much to be desired? For me, they became a turning point, a catalyst for deeper reflection and ultimately a loss of belief in the god they depict.

The doctrine of the Trinity is madness. Why does the church still want to hold to it? The doctrine of the Trinity is madness. Why does the church still want to hold to it? Because it’s convenient. It’s a theological sleight of hand, a way to reconcile the irreconcilable. How else can you explain a god who is simultaneously one and three? It’s like saying a square is also a circle if you just believe hard enough. The church clings to this absurdity because without it, the entire construct of Christian theology crumbles. If Jesus isn’t God, then his death wasn’t a divine sacrifice, and the whole salvation narrative falls apart. But let’s not mince words: the Trinity is a desperate attempt to patch together a story full of holes. It’s like trying to hold water in a sieve. The early church fathers knew this, which is why they cooked up the idea in the first place. It’s not in the Bible, not explicitly. It’s a later invention, a theological Band-Aid slapped on a messy, contradictory text. And yet, here we are, centuries later, still pretending it makes sense. Why? Because the alternative is too frightening for believers to face: that their faith might be built on sand, not rock. So they cling to the Trinity, a doctrine as logical as a unicorn with three horns, because admitting it’s nonsense would mean admitting that maybe, just maybe, they’ve been wrong all along. And that’s a pill too bitter to swallow. —Michael R. Burch

Does the Bible contradict itself? Does the Bible contradict itself? A resounding yes, and the evidence is as glaring as the sun on a cloudless day. From the very first verses of Genesis, the contradictions begin to mount. Was light created before the sun and stars, or after? The Bible can’t seem to decide. In one breath, Genesis claims that plants sprouted on the third day, long before the sun was created to nourish them with its light and warmth. How did photosynthesis work without sunlight? The Bible doesn’t bother to explain. Then there’s the matter of the flood. Was Noah to take two of every kind of animal, or seven? The Bible says both. Did the flood last 40 days or 150? Again, the text can’t make up its mind. Even the Ten Commandments, supposedly carved in stone by the finger of God, contradict themselves. In Exodus, God commands, “Thou shalt not kill,” yet just a few chapters later, He orders the Israelites to slaughter entire nations—men, women, children, and even the livestock. Is this a moral code or a blueprint for genocide? The Bible’s contradictions aren’t limited to the Old Testament. In the New Testament, the genealogies of Jesus in Matthew and Luke don’t match. Was Joseph’s father Jacob, as Matthew claims, or Heli, as Luke insists? The birth narratives themselves are at odds. Matthew says Jesus was born during Herod’s reign, while Luke claims it was during the time of Quirinius—a discrepancy of at least a decade. Even the resurrection accounts vary wildly. Was it one angel at the tomb, or two? Did the women tell the disciples immediately, or did they keep silent out of fear? The writers of the Bible can’t seem to agree on the details of the most pivotal event in Christian theology. These contradictions aren’t minor quibbles; they’re fundamental inconsistencies that undermine the Bible’s claim to divine inspiration. If God is the author of truth, why does His word read like a poorly edited first draft? The answer is simple: the Bible was written by humans, each with their own agenda, biases, and imperfect memories. It is a product of its time, not an infallible guide to morality or truth. To treat it as such is to ignore the glaring contradictions that pepper its pages. And yet, Christians continue to cling to the notion of biblical inerrancy, twisting logic and reason into knots to explain away the inconsistencies. But no amount of theological gymnastics can reconcile the irreconcilable. The Bible contradicts itself, and no amount of faith can change that fact. So, does the Bible contradict itself? Unequivocally, yes. And anyone who claims otherwise is either ignorant of the text or willfully blind to its flaws.
